source.title: One Modality to Forget Them All: Enhancing Cross-Modal Unlearning in Vision-Language Models
source.authors: S. Balaji; Yili Ren; Guang-Jing Wang; Yi-Min Chen; Ningzhuo Wang

record.file_problem: The full paper text, including appendices, is present. Some figures and tables are flattened in the web text, but the relevant numeric results are also stated in tables or prose.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests recovery of unlearned behavior with typographic image prompts, a different attack method in vision-language models. It also tests a proposed counter-method against that attack.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates typographic attacks that render harmful prompts as images, but does not test recovery by fine-tuning on a small relearning set, activation-direction ablation, post-unlearning low-bit quantization, or textual rephrasing, other-language prompts, or in-context information. QLoRA quantization is used for training, not as a post-unlearning recovery attack. CKA and intervention-point results are not direct tests of the specified activation-direction or access-versus-deletion mechanisms. Results cited from other studies are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study tests the claim in a new setting: safety unlearning of harmful behavior in three VLMs. It measures standard post-unlearning ASR and utility, then shows that black-box typographic image prompts elicit unsafe outputs from text-unlearned checkpoints. It also tests a new counter-method, CrossInf, against that attack. The measure is harmful-compliance ASR, not knowledge accuracy as in WMDP or Harry Potter.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that single-modality unlearning in VLMs transfers asymmetrically and is shallow: typographic attacks recover the majority of unlearned behaviors, a claim based on target-string rates. They say gradient ascent changes output tendencies without erasing knowledge. They state that CrossInf partially closes the transfer gap and brings LlamaGuard typographic ASR to 0% while keeping utility; target-string ASR stays nonzero.
record.recipe_differences: The vanilla baseline follows a three-term gradient-ascent unlearning loss with refusal training and retain-set KL, implemented with QLoRA. CrossInf applies that loss only to selected influential blocks. The paper does not test Who's Harry Potter, RMU, or post-unlearning quantization.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by architecture and fusion design; transfer direction matters. CrossInf performance varies with the model-specific top-k block selection and evaluation metric (target-string versus LlamaGuard).

fits_no_version.finding: Text-to-visual transfer of unlearning is strong, but visual-to-text transfer depends on the fusion architecture.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-modal transfer of unlearning depends on transfer direction and VLM fusion design.

fits_no_version.finding: LLM-only LoRA is the only single-component intervention that transfers cross-modally. LLaVA transfers despite cross-modal CKA of 0.95, which the authors call a boundary effect.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unlearning can transfer via output-layer decision boundaries without representational change.

record.problems: The attack evaluation uses three 7–9B VLMs and 90 typographic images. No never-saw-the-knowledge model is used to determine whether attack recovery exceeds that reference. The two automated metrics diverge, and the paper notes that LlamaGuard underreports residual unsafe behavior after unlearning. The study tests one standardized gradient-ascent QLoRA recipe, not the range of unlearning methods in the claim. It reports no error bars or confidence intervals for the ASR results.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant numeric results were omitted. The study’s intervention-point comparisons and CKA analyses do not directly test the specified activation-direction ablation or access-versus-deletion mechanism, so they were not included as version C rows.

untested.parts: Targeted-knowledge accuracy near chance (e.g. WMDP-style QA); never-trained reference models; text-only LLMs; methods other than gradient-ascent QLoRA (RMU, NPO, WHP).
Entirely untested; no relearning or fine-tuning attack after unlearning.
No activation-direction ablation. CKA and LoRA-magnitude analyses are descriptive and do not test blocking versus deletion.
No post-unlearning quantization attack; 4-bit loading is used for training only.

Text-only rephrasing, in-context information, and text jailbreaks against text-unlearned models. Multilingual and encoded variants exist only inside the typographic image set, with no per-category results.
CrossInf against fine-tuning, internal edits, quantization, or text prompting attacks; human-validated safety of CrossInf outputs.

missing.what: Intervention-point ablation: vision-only and fusion-only unlearning leave cross-modal text-probe ASR unchanged (e.g. LLaVA 0.736 to 0.736) while same-modal ASR drops. This bears on the incomplete-unlearning part of A.

CrossInf on visual-to-text transfer: LlamaGuard ASR for LLaVA falls from 13.9% to 1.4%, and IDEFICS/InstructBLIP to 0%; LLaVA target-string ASR rises from 40.3% to 43.1%. IDEFICS utility rises from 11.5% to 31.7%.

Human evaluation: human-judged ASR falls from 50.3% to 14.1% after unlearning; LlamaGuard false-negative rate is 49%, and 74% on post-unlearning outputs. This is needed to read the LlamaGuard-based rows.

record.verdict_notes: The 90-image typographic set has no pre-unlearning ASR, so 'recovery' is inferred only by comparison with post-unlearning FigStep. Table 4's bold best-k values differ from the k the text says was adopted (50/30/30), and were chosen on the test set itself. The human-evaluation claim that recovered typographic outputs are unsafe is asserted, not reported separately for Exp 3. The unlearning target is harmful-response behavior with refusal training, not factual knowledge, so A and E apply by analogy.

versions.untested_parts: Tests gradient-ascent-based QLoRA unlearning in three VLMs and typographic image attacks, not all current LLM unlearning methods or ordinary text-only LLMs. No never-saw-the-knowledge model is used as the recovery comparison.
No fine-tuning or relearning attack is applied after unlearning.
No activation-direction ablation is performed, and the reported representation analysis does not directly test whether unlearning blocks access rather than deletes knowledge.
No post-unlearning quantization attack is performed.
Tests typographic re-encoding of harmful prompts as images only; it does not test text rephrasing, jailbreak prompts, other-language text prompts, or in-context information.

Tests CrossInf against typographic attacks and cross-modal transfer in the evaluated VLMs; does not establish resistance to fine-tuning, activation edits, quantization, or the other untested prompt attacks.
